statement: Ben has three cards showing the digits 2, 5 and 8. He makes numbers by placing one, two or all three of the cards in a row. How many different numbers can he make?

choices.misconception: I only counted the numbers that use all three cards.
I counted which cards are used, 3 single cards, 3 pairs and 1 group of three, but forgot that changing the order makes a new number.
I counted the one-card and two-card numbers but forgot the numbers that use all three cards.
I counted the two-card and three-card numbers but forgot that a single card is a number too.

hints: Count the one-card, two-card and three-card numbers separately.
Systematic listing: for each length, list the numbers in order of their first digit so none is missed or repeated. Then add the three lengths.
One card: 2, 5, 8. Two cards: 25, 28, 52, 58, 82, 85. Three cards: there are 6.

solutions.reliable: One card: 2, 5, 8, that is 3 numbers. Two cards: 25, 28, 52, 58, 82, 85, that is 6 numbers. Three cards: 258, 285, 528, 582, 825, 852, that is 6 numbers. Total $3 + 6 + 6 = 15$. The transferable idea: split a listing by size and list each group in a fixed order, so nothing is missed.
solutions.elegant: For two cards: 3 choices for the first, 2 for the second, so 6. For three cards: $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$. Add the 3 single cards: 15.

whyOnTest: Organised listing, split by the number of cards used, is exactly what stops students missing or repeating cases.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
